parts:
The eigenvalues should be the same, but the eigenvectors are a little tricky.  When you don't have full rank, (n - r) of the eigenvectors will only be defined up to a subspace so that any linear combination of them will be fine.  I believe that Eigen (what we use internally) also ensures that the nominal eigenvectors for the deficient subspace are orthogonal, which is handy.

I can't vouch for the R implementation, but I have tested Eigen on these kinds of problems extensively and the eigenvalues always seemed reasonable.
On Mon, Nov 25, 2013 at 11:20 AM, Léa Fortunato <missp...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi,

I need to use the eigen decomposition of a symmetric matrix with rank (n-2). When comparing the eigen decomposition using R and Stan, the (3:n) values and vectors are completely identical. However, the 2 eigen values corresponding to the rank deficiency are different. And depending on the size of the matrix (n), the eigen vectors can be very different as well. Is it due to the algorithm?

Here is a toy example with R and Stan:

n<-30
P <- matrix(0, n, n); P[1, (1:3)] <- c(1, -2, 1); P[2, (1:4)] <- c(-2, 5, -4, 1); for(i in 3:(n-2)) { P[i, ((i-2):(i+2))] <- c(1, -4, 6, -4, 1) }
        P[n-1, (n-3):n] <- c(1, -4, 5, -2); P[n, (n-2):n] <- c(1, -2, 1)

P.eigen  <- eigen(P)

eigen_test <- '
data {
     int n;
     matrix[n, n] P;
}

transformed data {
    vector[n] eigenvalues_P;
    matrix[n, n] eigenvectors_P;
    eigenvectors_P <- eigenvectors_sym(P);
    eigenvalues_P <- eigenvalues_sym(P);
   
    print("eigenvalues= ", eigenvalues_P);
    print("eigenvectors[,1]=", col(eigenvectors_P,1));  //eigenvector[n] in R
    print("eigenvectors[,2]=", col(eigenvectors_P,2));
    print("eigenvectors[,3]=", col(eigenvectors_P,3));
 }

parameters {
   real y;
   }
  
model {
  y ~ normal(0,1);
  }
'

eigen_dat <- list(n=n, P = P)

fit <- stan(model_code = eigen_test, data = eigen_dat,  iter = 10, chains = 1)
